title: Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation
scenario: A 7-year-old boy with a history of asthma is brought to the emergency department by his mother for two days of worsening cough and audible wheezing that has not responded to his home rescue inhaler.

lines: 7-year-old male brought in by mother for 2 days of worsening cough and wheeze. Mother reports the boy has used his albuterol inhaler every 2 hours today without relief. Audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration, and suprasternal and intercostal retractions noted. Speaks in short 3-4 word phrases. Sitting upright in tripod position. Anxious but oriented. Known trigger is a recent upper respiratory infection.
Cardiorespiratory monitor and continuous pulse oximetry applied. IV access obtained. Chest x-ray and labs ordered. O2 started at 2 L per nasal cannula.
Continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium started per order. IV methylprednisolone administered. Child positioned high Fowler's.
Wheezing diminished with improved air movement in all lobes. Retractions resolved. Speaking in full sentences and playing on mother's phone. Nebulizer spaced to every 4 hours.
Albuterol HFA inhaler 2 puffs PRN wheeze
Montelukast 5 mg PO daily at bedtime
Continuous nebulized albuterol with ipratropium bromide
Oxygen to keep SpO2 greater than 94%
Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Notify provider for SpO2 less than 90% or rising PaCO2

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.rationale: Hypoxia, accessory-muscle retractions, difficulty speaking in full sentences, and marked tachypnea all signal severe airway obstruction and respiratory distress requiring prompt intervention.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it indicates worsening airway obstruction, impending respiratory failure, or both. Each finding may support more than one.

rows.text: Peak expiratory flow 45% of personal best

children.rationale: Wheeze and a reduced peak flow reflect airflow obstruction. A rising PaCO2 with acidosis and inability to speak in sentences reflect fatigue and CO2 retention, signaling impending respiratory failure as well.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem is {1}.

choices.text: impaired gas exchange from airway obstruction

children.rationale: The most immediate threat is impaired gas exchange from bronchospasm and obstruction, evidenced by hypoxia and a rising PaCO2; it takes priority over the real but less urgent problems of anxiety and infection risk.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this child.
children.rationale: Beta-agonists, systemic steroids, and upright positioning open the airway and improve oxygenation. Beta-blockers cause bronchoconstriction and withholding oxygen worsens hypoxia, so both are contraindicated.

children.subject: Pharmacology
children.stem: While the child receives continuous nebulized albuterol, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess air movement and breath sounds frequently
Keep the child NPO and restrict all fluids

children.rationale: Albuterol causes tachycardia and can lower potassium, so the nurse monitors heart rate, potassium, and airway response. Fluid restriction and stopping oxygen are not indicated.

children.subject: Pediatrics
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Peak expiratory flow remains 45% of personal best

children.rationale: Improved oxygenation, slower respiratory rate, absence of retractions, and return of normal speech all show the obstruction is resolving. A persistently low peak flow would indicate ongoing obstruction, not improvement.
